notes.title: Start here: a course disguised as an issue tracker
notes.body:
Tracer is a Linear-style issue tracker built as 15 annotated pull requests. The big story is a migration: Sprints 1-5 build a classic REST app with a query cache, then Sprints 6-7 replace it with a local-first sync engine.

This quest is built from the architecture decision records (ADRs) in `docs/adr/`. Each ADR has the same shape: context, decision, the alternatives that lost, and the consequences. Read the alternatives carefully: the guide says that if you cannot explain why the losing side lost, you have not learned the decision.

Suggested order: ADR-0003 (sessions), 0004 (cursor pagination), 0005 (fractional indexing), then the sync trio 0006, 0007 and 0008, and finally 0012 (what an incident drill taught). Each ADR ends with a Links list; open those files, because the quizzes ask what the code does.

excerpts.quote: keyboard-driven UX performance. Its central arc: we build the app as a *classic* REST + query-cache web app (Sprints 1–5), then **migrate it to a local-first sync engine** (Sprints 6–7). You watch a senior team replace an architecture under a live product. That's the most valuable thing here.

- **The planted debate.** Each PR has a design-decision thread with both sides argued and a resolution. Read the losing side charitably; if you can't explain why it lost, you haven't learned the decision. - **The ADRs** in `docs/adr/` — the durable "why" behind the architecture.

readMore.why: How to study the course: predict, review, then do the lab.
The wire protocol behind the sync ADRs.

notes.title: Two ideas behind the sync engine: a log and an overlay
notes.body:
The server side keeps a mutation log. Every write to an issue goes through one function, `recordMutation`, which numbers it within its workspace, stores it as a row and tells connected clients about it. While you read it, note the order of those steps and what a client can rely on when a message to it goes missing.

The client side keeps two layers: what the server has confirmed, and local edits the server has not confirmed yet. What you see on screen combines the two.

Keep both pictures in mind while reading ADR-0006 and ADR-0007, and open the pure functions in `packages/shared/src/store.ts`. They are small, have no network code, and are tested with property tests. For each function there, write down which layer it reads and which layer it changes: the ack path, the rejection path and the rebase path.

excerpts.quote: Two clients edit the same workspace; changes must appear on every screen live, survive reconnects, and stay consistent.
Sprint 07 makes the client offline-first: it must boot without the network, apply local edits instantly (optimistically), send them when connected

readMore.why: The single server write path for synced entities.
The client overlay model as pure functions.

notes.title: Ordering lists cheaply: keysets and fractional keys
notes.body:
Two ADRs solve an ordering problem without touching many rows.

ADR-0004 is about reading a long list page by page. Instead of page numbers, the server hands back an opaque token that encodes where the last page ended, and the next query starts strictly after that point using an index. Look at how the token is built and decoded in `apps/api/src/lib/pagination.ts`, and at the matching query in `apps/api/src/routes/issues.ts`.

ADR-0005 is about dragging an issue to a new position. Each issue has a string key, and keys compare as plain strings. To place an issue between two others you compute a new key that sorts between their keys. Open `packages/shared/src/order.ts` and trace `keyBetween` by hand for a couple of inputs before you take the quiz.

excerpts.quote: - **OFFSET/LIMIT.** Familiar page numbers. Rejected on two counts: (1) correctness — under concurrent inserts/deletes, OFFSET skips or repeats rows across pages (an issue tracker is constantly mutating); (2) performance — the database must scan and discard `OFFSET` rows, which is O(n) and degrades as you page deeper. Cursor pagination is stable under writes and stays O(log n) via the index.

// The alphabet is in ascending ASCII order so plain string comparison gives the right order. const DIGITS = "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"; const BASE = DIGITS.length; // 62

readMore.why: Why fractional keys beat integer positions and floats.

notes.title: Why the cursor needs the id tie-breaker
notes.body:
The list is ordered by `createdAt desc, id desc`, and the next page uses this keyset predicate: rows with `createdAt` before the cursor, OR rows with the same `createdAt` and a smaller `id`. If the cursor held only `createdAt`, the second branch could not exist, and any rows sharing the boundary timestamp but not yet shown would be skipped. ADR-0004 calls the tie-breaker mandatory.

- Jumping to numbered pages is wrong: cursors give "next page" only; that is the trade the ADR accepts.
- Encoding is not the issue: `encodeCursor` joins the two fields with "|" and base64url-encodes any string.
- Authorization is wrong: team access is checked by `requireTeamAccess`, not by the cursor.

excerpts.quote: ...(cursor ? [ { OR: [ { createdAt: { lt: new Date(cursor.createdAt) } }, { createdAt: new Date(cursor.createdAt), id: { lt: cursor.id } }, ], }, ]
- The cursor + ordering + index must stay in sync; the tie-breaker `id` is mandatory or rows with equal `createdAt` can be skipped.

notes.title: Why a malformed cursor just means the first page
notes.body:
`decodeCursor` base64url-decodes the text and splits it on "|". With no "|" there is only one part, so `id` is `undefined`, and the guard `if (!createdAt || !id) return null` returns null. Any thrown error is caught and also turns into null. In the route, a null cursor means no keyset predicate is added, so the query starts from the top.

- Throwing a 400 is wrong: the function catches errors itself, and BAD_FILTER is the code for a bad `filter` parameter.
- An empty id is wrong: the guard rejects a missing id instead of building a cursor.
- createdAt holding the whole text is wrong for the same reason: the guard returns before any object is built.

excerpts.quote: export function decodeCursor(raw: string | undefined): Cursor | null { if (!raw) return null; try { const [createdAt, id] = Buffer.from(raw, "base64url").toString("utf8").split("|"); if (!createdAt || !id) return null; return { createdAt, id }; } catch { return null; } }

notes.title: Tracing keyBetween("a", "b") digit by digit
notes.body:
The alphabet is `0-9`, then `A-Z`, then `a-z`, so "a" is index 36, "b" is 37 and "V" is 31. At position 0, x = 36 and y = 37. They differ, but their midpoint rounds down to 36, which equals x, so the function copies "a" and moves one position deeper. At position 1, "a" has no more characters (padded with 0) and "b" has none either (padded with 62), so the midpoint is 31: the result is "a" + "V".

- "ab" is wrong: its second digit is index 37, but the second digit comes from the midpoint of 0 and 62.
- "a5" is wrong for the same reason: that midpoint is 31 ("V"), not 5.
- The one-character "V" is what `keyBetween(null, null)` returns; with "a" and "b" as bounds the first digit must stay "a".

excerpts.quote: const DIGITS = "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"; const BASE = DIGITS.length; // 62

for (;;) { // Pad `a` with the minimum digit and `b` with one-past-max so nulls fall out naturally. const x = i < lo.length ? idx(lo[i]!) : 0; const y = i < hi.length ? idx(hi[i]!) : BASE; if (x === y) { out += DIGITS[x]; i++; continue; } const mid = Math.floor((x + y) / 2); if (mid === x) { // Digits are adjacent — copy this one and go deeper (the boundary tightens). out += DIGITS[x]; i++; continue; } return out + DIGITS[mid]; }

notes.title: Flaw #2: fractional keys that keep growing
notes.body:
ADR-0005 names the flaw itself: when you keep inserting between the same two neighbours, each new key is longer than the last. The source comment on `keyBetween` points to the fix, and `evenKeys` in the same file is that fix: in Sprint 12 it reassigns a whole column to evenly spaced keys of equal, short length, and `maxKeyLength` is the metric that tells you when to run it.

- Two clients minting one key is not flaw #2: at this point the server computes keys, and Sprint 07 resolves collisions through the sync engine, not a lock.
- Precision loss is the problem with floating-point positions, the alternative the ADR rejected.
- The alphabet is already in ascending ASCII order, so plain string comparison is correct.

excerpts.quote: - **Known flaw (#2):** keys grow in length without bound when you repeatedly insert between the same two neighbours. Fine at product scale; a rebalancing pass + a key-length metric land in Sprint 12.

/** * Rebalancing (S12, harvest of flaw #2). When repeated same-slot inserts have grown the keys long, * we reassign the whole column to `n` evenly-spaced, SHORT keys. The new keys are uniform length, * so future inserts between them start short again. A rebalance emits ordinary mutations (each issue * gets a new sortOrder), so it flows through the sync engine like any other change. */

notes.title: Why the fanout happens only after commit
notes.body:
`recordMutation` does its database work inside `prisma.$transaction`: it bumps the workspace sequence and writes the log row. Only after that resolves does it call `fanout.publish`. The comment gives the reason: if clients were told about a mutation before the transaction committed, a rollback would leave them showing a change that never happened.

- A deadlock is not the reason: publishing is an in-process call with no database lock.
- A commit timestamp is not used: order comes from the `seq` allocated in the transaction.
- Clients dropping early deltas is invented: nothing in the client checks indexing; the risk is showing state that rolls back.

excerpts.quote: * We publish AFTER the transaction commits: announcing an uncommitted mutation would let clients * see state that then rolls back.
fanout.publish(input.workspaceId, delta);

notes.title: Why a missed delta is never a lost change
notes.body:
ADR-0006 states the rule: the log is truth, the fanout is a hint. Each mutation is stored with a monotonic per-workspace `seq`. A client remembers the last `seq` it applied. When it reconnects or bootstraps, it asks for everything after that number and replays it. The source comment says a dropped publish is never a lost mutation.

- Server resends until ack is wrong: the fanout is fire-and-forget; recovery is the client's replay.
- Staying missing is wrong: replay from `lastSeq` fills the gap.
- Asking other clients is wrong: this is a server-ordered design, not peer-to-peer; ADR-0012 shows the same catch-up working when pub/sub died.

excerpts.quote: as a durable fact, and fans the delta out. Clients bootstrap from their `lastSeq` and then receive live deltas. **The log is truth; the fanout is a hint** — a client that misses a delta replays from its `lastSeq`.

* the seq is allocated atomically per workspace inside the same transaction — then fans the delta * out. Rule to memorize: the log is truth, the fanout is a hint. If a client misses the hint it * catches up by replaying from its lastSeq, so a dropped publish is never a lost mutation.

notes.title: Why rollback is just dropping a pending entry
notes.body:
The overlay store never changes `committed` for an optimistic edit. The edit is only an entry in `pending`. What the screen shows is `materialize(state)`: a copy of committed with each pending mutation applied on top. Remove the pending entry and the next materialize no longer includes the edit. ADR-0007 says it in one line: rollback means drop a pending mutation.

- An undo copy is wrong: there is nothing to restore, because committed was never touched.
- An inverse delta is wrong: the server does not send undo messages; it simply never confirms the edit.
- Reloading from IndexedDB is wrong: IndexedDB is for booting offline, not for rollback.

excerpts.quote: export function materialize<T extends Entity>(state: StoreState<T>): T[] { const view: Record<string, T> = { ...state.committed }; for (const m of state.pending) { if (m.op === "delete") delete view[m.entityId]; else if (m.value) view[m.entityId] = m.value; } return Object.values(view); }

The view is **`materialize(committed, pending)`**: committed truth with the pending overlay applied on top. **We never mutate committed optimistically.** Rollback = drop a pending mutation; rebase = re-materialize over new committed (automatic every render). A server delta whose `mutationId`

notes.title: What an ack does to a pending edit
notes.body:
When the server confirms an edit, its delta carries the same `mutationId` the client generated. Two pure functions handle it. `applyServerDelta` writes the server's value into `committed`. `ackMutation` filters the matching entry out of `pending`. After that, the screen shows the server's value from committed truth, and the optimistic copy is gone.

- Keeping the entry is wrong: it would shadow later foreign edits with a stale optimistic value.
- Ignoring the delta is wrong: committed must learn the server's value, which may differ under per-field LWW.
- Resending is wrong: the ack ends the mutation's life; resending happens only when no ack arrives.

excerpts.quote: /** Drop a pending mutation once its confirming delta (same mutationId) has hit committed. */ export function ackMutation<T extends Entity>( state: StoreState<T>, mutationId: string, ): StoreState<T> { return { ...state, pending: state.pending.filter((m) => m.mutationId !== mutationId) }; }
re-materialize over new committed (automatic every render). A server delta whose `mutationId` matches a pending one **acks** it (drops it from pending). The state lives in IndexedDB, so the app

notes.title: Why a resent create returns the first issue
notes.body:
The create handler checks for a `mutationId` first. If one is given, it searches the mutation log for that workspace and id. When it finds a match, it loads the issue that mutation created and returns it, instead of creating another row. ADR-0007 calls this exactly-once-in-effect: the client may send the create twice, but it takes effect once.

- 409 is wrong: the handler returns the existing issue as a normal success, so the client can ack it.
- A second issue is the bug this code fixes (the double-submit and ack-loss arc).
- 400 is wrong: resending the same mutationId is expected behaviour after a lost ack.

excerpts.quote: // Exactly-once-in-effect: if we've already applied this mutationId, return the existing issue // rather than creating a second one. This is the fix for the double-submit / ack-loss arc — a // client that resends because it never saw the ack must not end up with two issues. if (body.mutationId) { const seen = await prisma.mutationLog.findFirst({ where: { workspaceId: accessTeam.workspaceId, mutationId: body.mutationId }, }); if (seen) { const existing = await prisma.issue.findFirst({ where: { id: seen.entityId }, include: { state: true, assignee: true }, }); if (existing) return serialize(existing, accessTeam.key);

notes.title: Why only a hash of the session token is stored
notes.body:
`createSession` makes a random token, stores `tokenHash: hashToken(token)` with the user id and an expiry 30 days out, and returns the raw token for the cookie. `getUserByToken` hashes the incoming cookie value and looks up that hash. So a copy of the database does not contain usable cookies, and revoking a session is deleting its row (ADR-0003).

- The raw token is wrong: only the hash is written.
- A JWT copy is wrong: ADR-0003 rejected JWTs because they cannot be revoked instantly.
- An OAuth access token is wrong: OAuth is only used at sign-in; the session row holds no provider token.

excerpts.quote: export async function createSession(userId: string): Promise<string> { const token = randomToken(); await prisma.session.create({ data: { tokenHash: hashToken(token), userId, expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + TTL_MS) }, }); return token; }

export async function getUserByToken(token: string | undefined): Promise<User | null> { if (!token) return null; const session = await prisma.session.findUnique({ where: { tokenHash: hashToken(token) }, include: { user: true }, }); if (!session || session.expiresAt < new Date()) return null; return session.user;

notes.title: Why presence uses its own short-lived path
notes.body:
ADR-0008 sorts collaborative state by one question: does it need to be correct across devices and survive a reload? Comments do, so they go through `recordMutation` like any other entity. Presence does not. It is a heartbeat every few seconds per viewer and is useless moments later. Logging it would add huge numbers of rows, slow every bootstrap, and store data nobody queries, so it travels on an in-memory `presenceBus` and simply expires.

- Needing a team id is wrong: the log input declares `teamId: string | null` (mutations.ts:7), so a write with no team is accepted.
- Encryption is not mentioned anywhere in the decision.
- Other workspaces is wrong: presence is about viewers of one team, not cross-workspace delivery.

excerpts.quote: - **Presence is ephemeral → a separate, in-memory path.** Presence messages are broadcast over the same socket but on a distinct logical channel (an in-process `presenceBus`) and are **never written to the mutation log**. Stale viewers simply expire.

- **Put presence in the mutation log too** (uniformity). Rejected: presence is high-churn (a heartbeat every few seconds per viewer) and worthless a moment later — logging it would bloat the log with millions of "still here" rows an hour, slow every bootstrap, and record data no one will ever query. Durability is a *choice per state kind*, not a global policy.

notes.title: What the fanout drill actually found
notes.body:
The drill killed pub/sub in the middle of a collaboration session. Clients kept working from their local overlay, then caught up from `lastSeq` once they reconnected, so nothing was lost; updates were only late. The ADR says the real finding was elsewhere: the API reported itself healthy while fanout was dead, so nobody was paged. The decision adds a fanout-liveness alert and reconnect backoff with jitter instead of pub/sub redundancy.

- Lost edits is wrong: the overlay kept them and the log replay delivered the rest.
- A lagging log is wrong: the durable log was the part that kept working.
- A reconnect stampede did not happen; backoff with jitter is added to prevent one in future.

excerpts.quote: The fanout (Redis pub/sub, in the production topology) is a *hint*, not the source of truth — the `MutationLog` is truth (ADR-0006). The incident drill (S15) killed pub/sub mid-collaboration on staging and confirmed the design claim: clients kept working from their local overlay store, and on reconnect they caught up from `lastSeq` off the durable log. Nothing was lost; updates were merely delayed until reconnect.

- Add a **fanout-liveness alert** — the drill's real finding was that the API stayed "healthy" while fanout was dead, so no page fired. That gap, not the outage itself, was the incident. - Add **reconnect backoff with jitter** on the fanout client so recovery doesn't stampede.

notes.title: Beyond the sync trio: the bookend ADRs, two audits and the retro
notes.body:
The second half of this quest widens the reading list beyond the sync ADRs.

Start with the two bookend decisions written in Sprint 1: ADR-0001 picks the frontend shell and ADR-0002 lays out the migration roadmap that the whole course follows. Then read the three product-depth decisions: ADR-0009 (saved filters), ADR-0010 (the command palette's search) and ADR-0011 (accessibility for a keyboard-first, real-time UI).

Next come two audits in `docs/audits/`. Each is written audit-first: a ranked findings table, what was fixed in that PR, and what was deferred with a plan. Finally, `docs/COURSE-RETROSPECTIVE.md` closes the course and looks back at every sprint.

As before, read each ADR's alternatives section closely: most questions ask why the losing option lost, or what a consequence commits the team to.

excerpts.quote: Tracer is keyboard-first (command palette, single-key shortcuts) and real-time (issues move under you as teammates work).
Audit-first: measure and rank before touching code.

readMore.why: The closing look back at all fifteen sprints.

notes.title: Why Next.js lost: the server-render vs local-state split-brain
notes.body:
ADR-0001 gives three reasons for rejecting Next.js. An auth-gated tool gets almost no SEO benefit. Server rendering introduces a "split-brain" between what the server rendered and the local state, and that fights the local-first store built in Sprint 07. And the WebSocket/local-first story is simpler in a pure SPA.

- File-based routing is listed as a Next.js benefit, not a conflict; the keyboard registry is not mentioned.
- Caching one team's HTML for another team is not a concern the ADR raises.
- No extra WebSocket is described; the sync engine's socket is simply easier to reason about without SSR.

The context explains the stake: the client must boot from IndexedDB without waiting on a server render.

excerpts.quote: SSR introduces a server-render vs. local-state "split-brain" that fights the local-first store we build in S07

notes.title: When to revisit the SPA, and why the answer is a second app
notes.body:
ADR-0001's only revisit condition is a public, SEO-relevant surface, such as a marketing site or shared public boards. Even then the ADR does not reshape Tracer: that surface could live in a separate Next.js app.

- Slow first loads are not the trigger, and moving this app to Next.js is exactly the reshaping the ADR avoids.
- A mobile client appears only later, in the retrospective's v2 ideas, as something that shares `@tracer/shared`; it is not a revisit trigger.
- Offline bugs would argue against SSR, not for it: the shell boots from the local store first and reconciles with the server afterwards.

excerpts.quote: that could live in a separate Next.js app rather than reshaping this one.

notes.title: The classic app is a planned throwaway with a named endgame
notes.body:
ADR-0002 calls the classic REST + TanStack Query architecture of Sprints 1-5 a deliberate, planned throwaway: replacing it is the core lesson of the course. The endgame is named on day one so early decisions are made with it in view. The ADR's own examples are choosing a SPA (ADR-0001) and per-field mutation granularity, both because the sync engine will need them.

- It is not a lasting fallback: the TanStack Query layer is intentionally deleted in Sprints 06-07.
- It is not demo-only; early sprints are asked to keep their data layer at arm's length so the swap is clean.
- The two data layers do not ship side by side; one replaces the other.

excerpts.quote: The classic architecture is a deliberate, planned throwaway
choose a SPA (ADR-0001) and per-field mutation granularity precisely because the sync engine will need them.

notes.title: Why ADR-0002 will never be revisited
notes.body:
Most ADRs end with a condition that would reopen them. ADR-0002 says "never", and explains why: the classic-then-sync roadmap is a pedagogical decision, not a technical one that scale could overturn. It exists so the learner feels the limits of invalidate-everything before the sync engine arrives.

- No load test is cited; scale is exactly the kind of evidence the ADR says does not apply.
- Deleting the classic data layer is described as a feature ("the migration is the curriculum"), not as the reason the decision is locked.
- Meridian is mentioned in other ADRs as precedent for some trade-offs; it does not fix this roadmap.

excerpts.quote: this is a pedagogical decision, not a technical one that scale could overturn.

notes.title: A closed field enum keeps filter input out of column names
notes.body:
In ADR-0009 a filter is a typed predicate AST. The fields it may name form a closed enum that zod validates, so user input can never become a raw column name, and saved views store the AST as data. The ADR calls this safe by construction, in contrast to the rejected query-string or raw SQL fragment approach, which it calls an injection factory.

- Escaping names inside compileFilter is not the mechanism; there is nothing to escape when the set is closed.
- Saved views are one use of the AST, not a gate in front of the server.
- Prisma index checks are not mentioned; the ADR notes only that an AST makes it analyzable which fields need indexes.

excerpts.quote: The field set is a **closed enum**, validated by zod — user input can never become a raw column name.

notes.title: The palette merges two systems the user never sees
notes.body:
ADR-0010 splits the command palette in two and merges the results seamlessly. Commands are already in memory, so they are fuzzy-ranked locally and instantly, boosted by frecency. Issues may far outnumber what the client has loaded, so they come from a debounced server search across the user's teams, which covers that long tail.

- A server search cannot be the offline path; the local path is the one that is instant and offline-capable.
- Commands are not fetched from the server and issues are not ranked from IndexedDB; it is the other way round.
- There is no single shared server index cached per team; the two systems stay separate.

excerpts.quote: Issues come from a **debounced server search** across the user's teams — the long tail the local store hasn't loaded.

notes.title: The named trigger for swapping in a fuzzy-search library
notes.body:
ADR-0010 rejects Fuse.js and minisearch for now: the hand-rolled matcher is about 80 lines, adds zero bundle, and is fully tunable to identifier patterns. It does not leave the choice open-ended; it names the trigger to adopt a library: multi-field weighting across entity types growing past roughly 200 lines.

- Bundle size is a reason the library lost, not a threshold that brings it back.
- Ranking problems are handled as regressions pinned with fixtures, not counted toward a switch.
- The issues the client has not loaded are served by the server search, which is unrelated to the matcher.

excerpts.quote: names the trigger to adopt a library: multi-field weighting across entity types past ~200 lines.

notes.title: Scoped server search, personal client-side frecency
notes.body:
Two consequences in ADR-0010 pull in opposite directions. The server issue search is permission-scoped, so guests only search their own teams, because a search index that forgets scoping is a data-exfiltration API. Frecency, by contrast, lives on the client because it is your own muscle memory, not shared state.

- Speed, caching and ranking quality are not why scoping matters; the risk is leaking data a user cannot read.
- Frecency is not shared on the server, stored per team, or kept in Redis. It is persisted on the client for one user.

excerpts.quote: a search index that forgets scoping is a data-exfiltration API.
Frecency lives client-side (it's *your* muscle memory, not shared state).

notes.title: Shortcut help that cannot drift from the shortcuts
notes.body:
ADR-0011 generates the `?` help overlay from `useRegistry().list()`, the same registry that dispatches keys. Because behavior and documentation share one source, they cannot drift: adding a shortcut anywhere makes it appear in help for free. The consequences call the overlay a forcing function.

- A hand-maintained cheatsheet is the rejected alternative; it rots on the first forgotten update and cannot show which shortcuts are active in the current scope.
- No author writes help lines by hand, and no CI diff exists.
- Keyboard tests do not feed the overlay; the live registry does.

excerpts.quote: Behavior and documentation share one source, so they cannot drift.

notes.title: A polite live region, and the gap it cannot close
notes.body:
ADR-0011 routes announcements through one polite live region: the toast container. It rejects `aria-live="assertive"` because it would interrupt whatever the user is reading on every teammate keystroke; collaborative changes are informative, not urgent.

The consequence it states honestly: announcements are only as good as the events that reach the toast bus. A component that mutates the DOM silently still has to `show()` something, and the ADR calls that a review checklist item, not a guarantee.

- Nothing is announced automatically just because the DOM changed.
- The ADR never claims screen readers skip polite regions.
- Dropped toasts while typing are not discussed.

excerpts.quote: a component that mutates the DOM silently still needs to `show()` something.

notes.title: The theme cascade: explicit choice beats OS beats default
notes.body:
ADR-0011 themes the app with CSS custom properties in three tiers: `:root` holds the dark default, `@media (prefers-color-scheme)` follows the OS when the user has not chosen, and `[data-theme]` wins when the user makes an explicit choice. A swap is one attribute flip on `<html>`, and no component knows its own colors.

JS-driven inline theming was rejected because it couples color to components and defeats that single flip.

- `:root` is the lowest tier, not the winner.
- The OS preference applies only when no explicit theme is set.
- Radix was a separate rejected alternative about accessible components, not about theming.

excerpts.quote: Couples color to components and defeats the single-flip swap.

notes.title: Closing the WebSocket leak: team-aware delta forwarding
notes.body:
The Sprint 13 audit found that the WebSocket gateway built in Sprint 06 checked workspace membership and then forwarded every team's deltas, so a guest could read another team's issue titles from raw frames while REST correctly refused them.

The fix: every delta now carries the `teamId` it changed, and `canSeeDelta(membership, teamId)`, the same authz spine as Sprint 02, gates forwarding on both the live fanout path and the backlog stream. A regression test proves a guest sees only granted-team deltas.

- Rechecking workspace membership would repeat the coarse check that leaked.
- There is no socket per team.
- The backlog stream is filtered as well, not moved to REST.

excerpts.quote: Every delta carries the `teamId` it changed.

notes.title: The equivalence test the ADR promises is not in the tree
notes.body:
ADR-0009 admits that two implementations of one filter spec will drift unless a test forces them together. Read the pinned tests and that test is missing. `filter.test.ts` imports `evaluate` and nothing else, and both of its cases exercise the client evaluator. `compileFilter`, the function that turns the same AST into a Prisma where for `GET /issues`, is never called from any test.

That is the code-truth habit this quest keeps asking for: a decision record states an intention, and the tree shows whether it was kept. Here the drift guard exists only in prose, so a new filterable field wired into one evaluator would ship without a failing test.

- No fixture file is shared between the shared package and the api tests.
- The saved-views route has no test of its own.
- The only e2e spec is about the keyboard.

notes.title: The live delta path applies deltas in arrival order
notes.body:
The shared store package has a reducer that sorts deltas by seq before applying them, and a property test proves that shuffled input converges. The live client does not use it. In `useTeamIssues`, each delta from the socket is applied on the spot with `applyServerDelta`, which simply writes the delta's value for that entity. So if seq 7 arrives before seq 6, the older value is written last and stays.

The client also tracks `lastSeq` as the highest seq it has seen, so the late delta does not look like a gap and nothing asks the server again. The Sprint 13 audit's convergence guarantee is true of the tested reducer; the delivered live path has no seq check.

- There is no sort on the live path.
- No delta is skipped for being older.
- No re-bootstrap is triggered by out-of-order arrival.

excerpts.quote: Reduce a batch of deltas to committed state, applied in seq order regardless of arrival order.
Live deltas: patch committed truth, ack our own pending, persist to disk.
